notes: Research: MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) comes from Barbara Minto at McKinsey (1960s-70s), the grouping test inside the Pyramid Principle. It partitions a whole on ONE dimension so branches do not overlap (ME) and together cover the whole (CE). Classic uses: profit/cost trees, issue trees, market segmentation. Classic misuse: cutting on two dimensions at once (channel and geography) so items double-count; a catch-all 'Other' faking exhaustiveness; buckets that are MECE but carry no insight. Design decision: added one slot `cut` (typical_provenance derived) for the partitioning dimension, plus relation `cut_by` (whole -> cut). MECE's whole content is the choice of a single cutting dimension, and the registry itself says 'the partitioning principle is an LLM choice' inside the bucket description; giving it a node makes the choice inspectable and gives the tree its native four-level shape (whole / cut / buckets / items+gaps). All five registry slot ids and all four registry relations are kept. Scout returned three candidates: (1) the 2025-10-24 media-landscape map, (2) Elad Gil's AI-vertical partition on 2025-10-10, (3) the 2025-08-06 five levels of robotic autonomy. Chose (2): it is the only one with a stated whole carrying a size ($5T of services), a stated cut (vertical by vertical), named members per branch, a textbook exclusivity violation (the foundation model layer is filed as a branch and then re-appears inside the coding branch), and branches the speaker himself flags as unresolved. That gives the gap slot real work: the residual branch holding most of the $5T, the screen for verticals that never bought software (legal is the worked case), the labor half of every bucket, and the distinction between a branch with no winner and a branch with nobody in it. Candidate (1) had 14 buckets, no extraction coverage, and a weaker business angle; candidate (3) was cleaner to draw but its partition is quoted from someone else's published framework rather than built in the conversation.
